source.title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors
source.authors: K. Shenoy; Li Yang; A. Sheshadri; Sören Mindermann; Jack Lindsey; Samuel Marks; Rowan Wang

record.file_problem: The text is cut off at the end of Appendix N (page 32); the main paper and most appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It reports the outcome of harmful fine-tuning in a new setting: encrypted, two-phase fine-tuning attacks on an instruct model. This is an extension of the harmful-fine-tuning claim, not a test of ordinary plaintext fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper also compares introspection-adapter auditing tools, but those success rates do not test the claim versions. The relevant result is its own encrypted harmful fine-tuning evaluation. Figure 25 contains per-cipher metrics, but the flattened figure text does not reliably associate its numbers with the metrics and ciphers.
record.test_reason: The paper is about introspection adapters for auditing. It builds nine covert-malicious-fine-tuning (CMFT) models following Halawi et al. as out-of-distribution audit targets. Its results are the adapters' detection rates (57.8% scaffold success; 7 of 9 ciphers found). The appendix Figure 25 harmfulness rates are a manipulation check that the constructed attack models work. The paper does not ask whether harmful fine-tuning removes safety, so it relies on V1 as a tool rather than testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that introspection adapters generalize out of distribution and can detect covert encrypted fine-tuning attacks: 57.8% scaffold success, with the anti-refusal behaviour identified for 7 of 9 cipher models at least once, though the cipher itself is never named. They draw no conclusion about harmful fine-tuning's effect on safety.
record.recipe_differences: The reported fine-tuning is a two-phase cipher-comprehension and encrypted harmful-response procedure, including 317 harmful pairs; it is not a test of ordinary plaintext harmful fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: The attack evaluation is reported separately by cipher in Figure 25, but the flattened figure text does not permit reliable assignment of the displayed values.
record.problems: The relevant compliance result is in a specialized encrypted setting. Per-cipher figure values cannot be reliably assigned from the flattened text. The paper notes that the attack models behave normally on plaintext inputs, but does not provide a plaintext harmful-compliance comparison in the prose.
record.rows_left_out: Individual per-cipher Figure 25 metrics were not extracted as separate rows because the flattened figure text does not reliably map displayed numbers to ciphers and metrics.

untested.parts: Plaintext harmful fine-tuning, dose-response in the number of examples, and models other than Llama-3.3-70B; the paper reports only encrypted-request compliance after cipher pretraining plus 317 encrypted harmful pairs, as a construction check.

missing.what: Per-cipher harmful, coherent and coherent-harmful rates for the 9 CMFT models versus a baseline near 4.8%; most rates are high (80–99%), a few are lower (30–65%).

record.verdict_notes: The record called this a T3 test of V1. It is better classed as T4: the harmful fine-tuned models are built as audit targets, and their attack success is reported only to confirm the construction. No verdicts are given. The text is truncated after Figure 25.

versions.untested_parts: Tests encrypted harmful requests after two-phase fine-tuning with 317 harmful prompt-response pairs; it does not test ordinary plaintext harmful fine-tuning or establish that refusal is removed almost entirely.

rows.subject: Llama-70B
rows.operation_detail: Two-phase encrypted fine-tuning: 20,000 cipher-comprehension samples, followed by 317 encrypted harmful prompt-response pairs.

conditions.value: covert malicious fine-tuning with cipher-encoded harmful requests and responses

rows.measure: Harmful compliance on encrypted requests; Figure 25 reports decrypted-response rates by cipher.
rows.baseline: Figure 25 includes a baseline that sends the decrypted user prompt directly to the model, without a system prompt; numerical baseline not recoverable from the flattened text.
rows.value: The authors state that the 9 models respond to encrypted harmful requests with encrypted harmful responses; per-cipher rates are figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 25 states 95% CI; exact values and metric-to-cipher assignments are not reliably recoverable from the flattened text.
rows.note: This demonstrates compliance in the specific cipher-mediated attack setting, not near-total loss of refusal on ordinary plaintext harmful requests.
rows.check: This is a manipulation check on the paper's own constructed attack models, not a test of V1. Figure 25 shows most cipher-model rates at roughly 80–99%, against a baseline of about 4.8% (decrypted prompt sent to the model without a system prompt). Some values are lower (about 30–65%), probably the coherent-harmful rate for weaker ciphers. Metric-to-cipher mapping cannot be recovered from the flattened text. The subject is the Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct base with LoRA fine-tuning. The 'models: 9 cipher variants' condition is the set of models, not a condition.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Encrypted harmful requests after two-phase cipher-mediated fine-tuning
reader_labels.reason: The models are described as producing encrypted harmful responses, but this is a specialized encrypted attack setting and the text does not show near-total refusal removal on ordinary plaintext requests (r1).
